title: Loving My Country
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads from Claude Anshin Thomas's memoir At Hell's Gate, a Soviet-free Vietnam veteran's account, in the week after the presidential vote. Nomon opens with a supermoon lost behind rain clouds, then seen at 5:30 one morning glowing through clouds and trees, and asks whether the dark days are really new. Nomon wonders what it would mean to learn to love our country without sorting everyone into liberal or conservative. Thomas's passages describe rain that returns him to the monsoon fighting, and a father who beats his young son and says it is because of love. Nomon ends by asking everyone not to be too quick to think they know what is going on, since finding out may only happen together.

sentences.text: It's been unbelievably successful, with no fuss and no trouble.
Anyone would have thought this.
We've already sent them more than $2,000, which is a lot of Kenyan shellings.
Then I put out the basket at a mindfulness retreat I was giving in October, and I raised another $1,200, which we can send them.
The pump has been purchased.
You can look on our website under support, where I put a page about this.
The pump has been purchased and tested, and there are pictures of Marcy's older brother, Wellington, testing out the pump.
Marcy's younger sister, Danetta, is now in Nairobi.
She applied for university, and she's going to take a course in how to use a computer at Marcy's suggestion, so she'll know how to use a computer a little better.
You're going to have a lot of chances to use a computer in a small village in western Kenya.
Anyway, we did something there.
This is life-changing, something.
And I'm sure as we go along, each of us, and maybe different groups of us, will get together in different ways of helping this world.
The other evening was supposed to be a supermoon, as you maybe know.
The moon was going to be, or was, I suppose, as close as it's been to the earth since 1948, and would never be this close again until 2038.
So, not to be missed.
I was picturing seeing this beautiful, huge moon hanging in the beautiful cloudless sky with stars.
I was picturing, I'll set up the tripod and try to take a photo with the telephoto lens.
I got excited about the supermoon, and maybe a little desire, desiring a certain experience that I was picturing.
Then, not too unusual for here, it was cloudy, it was raining.
At least a couple of times I checked, it was all cloudy.
Maybe it cleared up in the middle of the night.
I wasn't serious enough to get up in the middle of the night and look.
But I looked up at the moon behind the clouds and the rain, and I hardly even saw it.
I didn't really look.
Mostly what I registered was disappointment.
I wasn't seeing what I wanted, didn't get what I wanted.
And of course for so many of us, for the last eight days, we've been thinking and feeling in all kinds of ways about unexpected things, not what we wanted, many of us.
So I was thinking about that in the light of the supermoon.
The full disclosure is that, not too surprisingly, probably if you know me, I'm on the liberal side of that equation.
But I hope that some reflections about this are useful to us regardless of who we voted for or if we voted at all.
We're so-called liberal or so-called conservative, as if there could be only two species, two subspecies of American.
And yet we think that way.
But the minute we think that, we realize how ridiculous and limited that view is, how narrow, that there could only be two views.
People have all kinds of reasons for choosing one thing or the other, including choosing to vote for one candidate or another candidate, or choosing not to vote at all.
This morning I got up early and went out to my backyard meditation hut to practice.
The other full disclosure is that for the last eight days, I found it really hard to keep up my daily practice at home.

I skipped several days, and sometimes I would tell myself, well, it's okay, because I'm going to be teaching a class or going to a retreat or being with somebody later on, and we'll be doing meditation or mindfulness or something.
Which was true enough, but it's really not the same.
It doesn't serve that same essential purpose as sitting quietly at home in the early morning, just to be there, just to be still before I launch into the day.
The other reason I haven't been very regular is I haven't been feeling that well, and maybe most of us haven't been feeling that well.
Maybe a little bit physically ill in the body, a little queasy, a little low energy, but mostly a lot confused and sick at heart and tense.
I've been studying the emotion of anger with somebody lately and realizing that my anger style is non-anger, is sort of hiding from anger.
So maybe there's anger there that I'm hiding from.
That's entirely possible.
But just trying to make sense of what's happening, and at the same time trying to be helpful to others, trying to help others make sense of it.

Maybe sometimes trying a little too hard to reassure others, and other times feeling shut down and not wanting to engage, wanting to hope that everything is okay somehow, and other times batting down wisps of despair that everything is very much not okay.
And then again, this paralyzing belief that there can only be two possibilities: either things are okay or things are not okay.
That doesn't make sense.
It couldn't be that simple, but we think that way.
This morning I somehow got myself right out of bed at 5:30 and said, "Okay, go sit, Tim."
I didn't make a big deal about it in my head, I just went.
And I saw the moon again.
Not rainy this time, still partly cloudy.
The moon was hanging just above the horizon to the northwest, on its way down for the day.
This white, beautiful orb shining through clouds and trees.
You could just make out some of the details of the surface and the craters.
Mostly this quality of just glowingness.
I stopped.
I really stopped somehow, and I really saw the moon.
The supermoon was there.
It was still there, showing itself in that particular way at that particular moment, and I was available that time.
It wasn't what I originally wanted in my supermoon experience, and that was okay.
It was incredibly beautiful, just as it is.
I've heard plenty of people, mostly those in my own liberal-leaning circles, talking like this is the beginning of a dark time.
Dark days are upon us.
We have to be strong.
We need to mobilize.
There's much to do.
We have been complacent.
That anger and frustration needs to be channeled and used as important energy.
And I've heard doubts about the usefulness of peacefulness.
We shouldn't chill out too much.
We shouldn't accept this.
We need our hard edge to be strong and be motivated to show up.
I was thinking about this, and the strange thing of course is that the America of a week ago Monday was more or less the same America as Tuesday night or Wednesday morning early.

So either the dark days have been with us already, maybe the dark days have been with us a long time, maybe the dark days have always been with us, because it doesn't seem quite right to say that the days are suddenly dark.
The days are dark and light.
The moon is clear sometimes, obscured by clouds other times.
It's still the moon.
This is still our beautiful, diverse, strong country.
Still our messed-up, mixed-up, desire-ridden, racist, confused country.
I was thinking part of this liberal ethos that I bought into is that it's a little bit suspicious to love our country.
Like loving our country is code for a certain kind of narrow-mindedness, a certain kind of political perspective.
A kind of nationalism, or even violence.
And I guess it can be, but maybe it's time for all of us, no matter where we are in the kaleidoscope of views, to actually learn how to love our country.
Maybe it's time to learn how to do that.
And what is our country anyway?
Is it an idea?
Is it the lands and peoples that live in it, that live in it now?
Or is it from before?
Or is it the hope of the future of our country?
What is this country, if we could love our country?
And maybe what this really means is it's time to learn effective ways to love everyone and everything.
That's the hope that I want to nurture, like the little candle flame I want to nurture.
It might be that our practice has something important to contribute.

This experiential training, this slow, patient training in unspooling our heart and dipping into the deep levels of suffering and confusion and incredible insight and light and clarity that our practice supports us in.

I was just talking to somebody: it is interesting that on the one hand it does seem to be true that there's an international rising of nationalist politics and all that, which is frightening and dangerous.
At the very same time, meditation practice has more traction than it's had in the history of time.
So that's interesting.
It may be very small, but may be very important.

Regardless of whether we're in a position to in some formal way bring some of the sensibilities and practices of meditation or mindfulness or compassion forward, somehow we've been supported by it in our lives.
We are privileged to have that deep, deep support.
So I think the bar is high for us, that the world is calling on us to learn a lot of wisdom here and a lot of compassion and really manifest that in practice.
So I think we need a much bigger vision than during dark times.
It might be that some of us, and even some of our teachers, were a little too quick to try to make sense of all this and put words to all this.
Some of what's been written and spoken, even by really wise people I respect, has been a little narrow, a little dualistic in that way.
A little simplistic.
So while sitting on our cushions and bringing our attention back to our breathing with kindness, will that solve anything exactly?
Well, not exactly, maybe.
But I really think it's important.
And we probably really need to renew our commitment to that, in a gentle way, not doing violence to ourselves.
In a gentle way, recommitting to this.

Because to have that as a part of our life, whether it's a private, quiet thing we do at home, whether it's something that we're very public about or somewhere in between, to have this practice in our life is to show a certain kind of stability, a certain kind of broad understanding and a certain kind of love.

And of course this includes all the emotions and all the thoughts and all the learning from the past and the wondering what's going to happen in the future, the being skillful, the choosing where to put our energy and our resources and our time.
It includes anger and it includes despair and it includes fear, of course.
We can't wall that off.
But can we find a way to be with all this that's honest and loving?
Because just letting the anger and fear spill out into the world, what's that going to do?
Just add to the trouble.
So my secret hope is, from the surprise of all this or the shock of all this, that we'll all be so deeply moved and motivated to find our way of expression around this.
How can each of us contribute to the future that we want, to the present that we want?
Whether that is mostly renewing our attention to the quiet work that we're already doing, that's wonderful.
Can we do that better?
More clearly, more lovingly, more kindly, more wisely?
Helping our families, helping our friends, helping our colleagues.
Or maybe it expresses in risk-taking and doing entirely new things that we never did before.
Sometimes it can be surprisingly smooth and easy, like telling a story of my travels and putting out a basket, and suddenly a young woman goes to college who didn't get to go to college before.
Sometimes it's not that hard, surprising.
Sometimes it's really hard and dangerous.
So that's my hope.
I hope that somehow the insights of our practice will help us.

And especially our style of practice maybe can really help us with the important, important, important point of not falling into these simplistic, binary, self, other, them, us, conservative, liberal, good, bad traps.
Maybe we can model a more subtle understanding that will really help people, because none of this is going to go anywhere if we can't get beyond that.
So I can actually understand if one of you or some of us in this room voted for Mr.
Trump.
I really can.
And it's perfectly fine.
This is what democracy is about, right?
We get to choose.
Our choices may have been a little limited there, but we get to choose.
And I'd love to know other reasons.
I'd love to understand more.
All this reveals how little I understand, doesn't it, how little we understand of each other and our choices and motivations and our views.
So I hope we can support in each of us the change that we hope to be making and the choices that we choose to make.
None of this can work if it's all a subtle way to make others like us.
At the same time all this was happening, a mindfulness student sent me a book called *At Hell's Gate, A Soldier's Journey from War to Peace*, which is a book I knew about, but I had never read.
One of the many on my outer lists.
Do you have [unclear: "a guy you're entering your outer book list that you count someone not getting around to reading"]?
This is a fellow named Claude Thomas.
On the cover he says his name is Claude Anshin Thomas, because Anshin is his Dharma name, like us.
He's a Soto Zen practitioner, an ordained practitioner.
I thought I'd share with you a little bit of Claude Anshin Thomas' book.
He was a Vietnam veteran, he is a Vietnam veteran.
Well, I won't say too much, because we should just let his words talk to us.
But he's a Vietnam veteran who, as we just found out, somehow ended up being a Zen priest and spending now all of his life working for peace.
Here's a little bit from Claude Thomas, Anshin, at Hell's Gate.
*Imagine for a moment you're standing outside in the rain.
What do you typically think and feel as the rain falls around you?
For me, every time it rains I walk through a war.
For two rainy seasons I experienced very heavy fighting during the monsoons in Vietnam.
The tremendous volume of water leaves everything wet and muddy there.
Now when it rains I'm back to walking through the fields of young men screaming and dying.
I see tree lines disintegrating from napalm.
I hear 17-year-old boys crying for their mothers, fathers, and girlfriends.
Only after re-experiencing all that can I come to the awareness that right now it's just raining.
For lack of a better word, let's call these events flashbacks.
They are a reliving of experiences that I have not yet come to terms with.*
*I could be in a grocery store reaching up to take a can of vegetables off the shelf when I'm suddenly overwhelmed by a fear because I think the can might be booby-trapped.
Rationally I know this isn't true, but for one year, one year, my tour of duty in Vietnam, I lived in an environment where this was a realistic fear.
To this day I am unable to process that wartime experience.
But this is not just my story.
This happens every day all over the world.
Every day there are people reliving war, reliving their own experiences of violence, calamity, and childhood trauma.*
*Before we can get to a place of peace we have to touch our suffering.
Embrace it and hold it.
This is something I've been learning in recent years.
For many years before that, all I learned, all I knew, was how to make war.
For my first 17 years, almost all my experiences watered the seeds of violence in me.
War was everywhere.
I was raised in a small town in Pennsylvania.
My father, like most of the men in the town, had served in World War II.
When that generation talked about war, they didn't speak truthfully, however, unable to touch the deep and profound wounds that war left inside them.
They talked about war like it was a great adventure.*
*So when I turned 17, and my father suggested I go into the military, I didn't question it.
I also didn't know much about politics.
It wasn't part of my life.
Now I understand how important it is to know what is going on in the world.
Though no long-term solutions to our world's problems are achieved through political ideologies completely, I was impacted by them, as each of us is, and a dear price is paid out of ignorance.

Today I understand that my father and the men and women of his generation were filled with illusions and denial about how deeply they are affected by their military service and by their war experiences.
I volunteered to go to Vietnam because I thought it was the right thing to do.
I didn't understand the nature of war or the nature of violence.*
*Three days after I was in country, I began to understand.
It was insane.
It's difficult to describe what I saw.
I could and still can taste and smell it and see the emptiness in everyone's eyes.
It was like being in a surreal horror movie.
During basic training, I was taught to hate.
On the firing range, we were shooting at targets that resembled people.
We were learning to kill human beings.
We had to be taught how to do that.
That's the work of the military.
The work is done in a variety of subtle and not-so-subtle ways.
When we were done on the firing range, we were supposed to stack our weapons in a certain way.
One day, as I was preparing to place my rifle carefully on the stack, I slipped.
I dropped it.*

*The drill instructor, a Sergeant First Class, screamed and cursed that I wasn't looking after my rifle properly, that my rifle was the most important thing in my life, because whether I lived or died depended on it.
This guy was 6 feet 3 inches to my 5 feet 8 and a half.
He stood in front of me with his chest jammed against my face, stabbing me with his fingers, screaming obscenities at me.
Then he pulled out his penis and urinated on me in front of everyone.
And then I was not allowed to wash for two days.
I felt shame at such a deep level.
I couldn't begin to handle it.*
*But if I hadn't been prepared for this military training by the rest of my life, but I had also been prepared for this by the rest of my life, that kind of teaching would have taken hold.
Oh, excuse me, let me reread that.
If I hadn't been prepared already for this kind of training, this kind of dehumanizing by the rest of my life, that kind of teaching would have taken hold.
As a young man, I was encouraged to fight, to be prejudiced and nationalistic.
I was taught that the way to solve problems was through violence.
If there was a conflict, the strongest person won.
And this is how it should be.
I learned this from my mother, my father, my teachers and my friends.*
*At the age of 5, I was living with my parents in an apartment that was part of the [unclear: "state"].
My father was a teacher and my mother took in laundry, cleaned houses and sometimes worked as a waitress or a barmaid to make ends meet.
One day I wanted to ride my bicycle and my mother didn't want me to.
But I was so excited and being a kid, I was persistent.
My mother's response was to push me and my bicycle down a flight of stairs. 20 steps.
Why I wasn't seriously injured, I don't know.
Kids are flexible, I guess.
And they learn quickly.
This wasn't a one time event.
My mother often reacted with violence.*
*My father was an emotionally hidden person.
Most of the time, alcohol, tobacco and other intoxicants provided the bonding agents that held the walls of repression in place.
But as is always the case, repression doesn't really work as a strategy for dealing with strong emotion.
And some of what's hidden squeezes out.
In the town where I lived, there was a lake.
And in the springtime, the water level would rise because of snowmelt.
One day when I was around 8, I went out to play.
I'd been given a pair of new tennis shoes with a clean and distinctive tread.
That day I was supposed to be home at 4 o'clock.
But what does a child know about time?*
*When I didn't come home at 4, my father got concerned and went looking for me.
He went down near the lake and he saw small footprints going into the water and not coming back.
And the footprints resembled the tread of my new pair of tennis shoes.
He became terrified with the thought that I had fallen into the lake and drowned.
He came rushing back.
And when he got home, I was already there.
He immediately took me into the bathroom.
Pulled down my pants.
Took out his leather belt and beat me until I was black and blue and bleeding from the middle of my neck to my ankles.
From the middle of my neck to my ankles.
I didn't take that in the first time.*
*In the middle of what he was doing, he realized that he was hurting me.
And he stopped.
Stopped beating me and started to doctor the wounds.
As he was doing this, he told me that he had beaten me because he loved me.
All the time he was dressing my wounds.
He kept repeating that he had done this because he loved me.
Because he loved me so much.
This was beginning of a long term association.
I learned that love equals violence.
I don't believe my father's intention was to hurt me.
He just could not be afraid.
He could not stand to feel the reality of his powerlessness.
So he expressed his fear through the only feeling he could access.
Anger.*
*Unable to understand or tolerate the intensity of his emotions, he chose to see his problems as external.
That all he needed to do was control the perceived source of his distress.
He was violent because he was not able to touch his own suffering.
And therefore, his suffering was acted out on others.
In this case, on me.
My mother was also unable to have honest access to her feelings.
To look at her suffering and her pain became violence towards me.
From an early age, I was taught that if I loved my country, I had to be ready to fight and die for it.
When I went into military training, I had volunteered.
I volunteered to fight in Vietnam.
They told me I was going there to bring peace.
And peace is accomplished at the point of a gun.
Why would I have believed any different?*
*When I finished high school, I went directly into the military.
I had been offered an athletic scholarship at a university when my father urged me to turn down the offer.
Because he said, you're not stable enough.
You just go flunk out.
You're too wild.
And later it says, you should go into the military.
It'll help you become a man.
I ended up joining the military really because I didn't know what else to do.
My father suggested it, and he was my father.
Even an absent father is a powerful figure in a family's life, especially his sons.
And he and his friends had fought in the Second World War.
And they would sit around and get drunk and tell stories that made war seem glamorous and exciting.*
*I remember the day I left for military service.
My father drove me to the bus station in Erie, Pennsylvania, a distance of 25 miles from home.
I had a little brown suitcase, a Boy Scout suitcase.
My name was written on it in black magic marker.
My father took me to the station, bought me a ticket, and left.
There was no goodbye hug, no handshake, no parting words.
He just left.
And I went numb.*
So somehow he survives a year in Vietnam, mostly by getting really good at it, through competence.
And then he talks about spending the next 25 years or so a wreck.
Unable to hold on relationships or jobs, he gets through college, and then eventually somehow stumbling across meditation.
And gradually his life starts to change.
Read a little bit of what he realized later.
*What happened to me in Vietnam is not unique.
Other people from different wars can identify with what I'm talking about.
Even people who have never fought in a war but are veterans of violent homes, violent cultures, deep confusion.
Even though the details and the particular events may be entirely different, there's something in my story that resonates with many people that offers an opening for us when we begin to talk.
When I talk, I'm telling my story, but I'm also telling the collective story.
I'm telling the story of hundreds of generations of millions of people affected by war and violence.
And what is important about telling it is not so much the details of the story, or even that it's my story, but of the telling itself.*

*Whenever I tell my story, it not only forces me to realize what has happened to me, it also brings me more in tune with the reality of interdependence and interconnectedness, with what Thich Nhat Hanh calls interbeing.
I see that certain events happen to me, and that these events have a clear impact on my psychological and physical existence and an impact on everyone I encounter.
These events shaped it, and because of these effects, I'm not living my life freely, I'm living in it as dictated by my suffering.
So I want to have some choice and some freedom in my life and help others.
I knew, I learned, that I need to wake up to the reality of these experiences.
How they affect my life, how I act them out, or how they become acted out through my person.
And then acknowledge my responsibility in all of this.*
*I find that as I begin to become more awake to the reality of my own life, I stop blaming others.
I can feel very alone in this journey because it is in fact a journey that only I can take.
But I don't have to take the journey alone.
Telling our stories, sharing them, can lead to the creation of community, a loving community, committed to really living life differently.
A community of like-minded people, not the same but with a shared intention.
And these people can get together, they can assist, they can help, support, they can encourage each other in the process of waking up.*
*This connection, this connecting, can and will manifest itself in many different ways.
Sometimes we help each other through sitting together, sometimes through touching and holding, nurturing, sometimes through talking.
We can support each other through serving as examples.
And we can help our community by taking principled actions for peace.*
So there's a little bit from Claude Thomas.
Powerful stuff.
So it was really wonderful to hear about, I don't know how many of you were there last week, but what a wonderful conversation it sounds like you had for hours.
So that's important.
We need to talk together.
It's also important to appreciate the support of our formal forms.
The formal talk is another way of being together.
Sitting silently together is another way of being together.
And I think the biggest thing I'm thinking right now is let's not be too quick.
Let's not be too quick to think we know what's going on, because I think we don't.
Neither should we be too dumb, as best we can.
Maybe the only way we can find out is finding out together, being together with everyone.
So thank you for listening to all that.
